# 1 Introduction

The **0–1 knapsack problem** is a classical combinatorial optimisation problem.
Given $n$ items with weight $w_i$ and value $v_i$, we choose whether to include
each item ($x_i \in \{0,1\}$) to maximise the total value:

$$
\max \sum_{i=1}^{n} v_i x_i
\text{subject to } \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i x_i \le W.
$$

The problem is NP-hard. Exact approaches can therefore become computationally
expensive for large inputs. In this lab we build the `knapsack` R package and
study three approaches with different performance characteristics:

| Algorithm | Exact? | Time complexity |
|:--|:--:|:--|
| `brute_force_knapsack()` | Yes | $O(2^n)$ |
| `knapsack_dynamic()` | Yes | $O(nW)$ for integer capacity $W$ |
| `greedy_knapsack()` | No | $O(n\log n)$ when sorting dominates |

We test their correctness and runtime, profile bottlenecks using profvis.

Alongside the 3 core algorithms, we implement and ship the optional parallel brute‑force search within the package.
This parallel implementation keeps the same asymptotic complexity $O(2^n)$ as serial brute force, and may reduce wall-clock runtime by distributing computation across multiple CPU cores.

Benchmarks are reported separately from profiling so that speedups can be calculated from measured execution times rather than assumed.

# 2 Data

The package includes `knapsack_objects`, a reproducible data set with 2000 items.
The code used to generate it is shown below for reference and is not rerun
when knitting the vignette.

```{r data-generation, eval=FALSE}
suppressWarnings(RNGversion(min(as.character(getRversion()), "3.5.3")))
set.seed(42, kind = "Mersenne-Twister", normal.kind = "Inversion")
n <- 2000
knapsack_objects <- data.frame(
  w = sample(1:4000, size = n, replace = TRUE),
  v = runif(n = n, 0, 10000)
)
# From the root of the package, save the data if it is not already included:
# usethis::use_data(knapsack_objects, overwrite = TRUE)
```

```{r load-data}
library(knapsack)
data("knapsack_objects", package = "knapsack")
stopifnot(exists("knapsack_objects"))
head(knapsack_objects)
```

There are `r nrow(knapsack_objects)` items. Weights are integers from 1 to 4000,
and values are generated uniformly between 0 and 10000.

# 3 Three methods

## 3.1 Brute-force search

The brute-force method enumerates possible item subsets and selects the best
feasible combination.

```{r brute-force}
brute_force_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:8, ], W = 3500)
brute_force_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:12, ], W = 3500)
brute_force_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:8, ], W = 2000)
brute_force_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:12, ], W = 2000)
```

**Question 1: How much time does it take for $n=16$ objects?**

```{r brute-force-time}
bf_time <- system.time(
  bf_result <- brute_force_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:16, ], W = 2000)
)
bf_time
```

With $n=16$, there are $2^{16}-1=65535$ non-empty subsets. The measured elapsed
time on this machine is **`r round(unname(bf_time["elapsed"]), 3)` seconds**.
The brute-force method scales exponentially, $O(2^n)$.

## 3.2 Dynamic programming

Dynamic programming exploits integer weights and reuses results for smaller
subproblems. With $m[i,c]$ denoting the maximum value achievable from the
first $i$ items with capacity $c$, the recurrence is

$$
m[i,c] =
\begin{cases}
m[i-1,c], & w_i > c,\\
\max\{m[i-1,c],\;m[i-1,c-w_i]+v_i\}, & w_i \le c.
\end{cases}
$$

```{r dynamic}
knapsack_dynamic(x = knapsack_objects[1:8, ], W = 3500)
knapsack_dynamic(x = knapsack_objects[1:8, ], W = 2000)
```

**Question 2: How much time does it take for $n=500$ objects?**

```{r dynamic-time}
dp_time <- system.time(
  kd <- knapsack_dynamic(x = knapsack_objects[1:500, ], W = 3500)
)
dp_time
kd$value
```

For $n=500$ and $W=3500$, approximately $500\times3500=1.75$ million
states may be considered. The measured elapsed time is
**`r round(unname(dp_time["elapsed"]), 3)` seconds**. This is a
pseudo-polynomial-time algorithm with complexity $O(nW)$.

## 3.3 Greedy heuristic

The greedy method ranks items by value-to-weight ratio ($v_i/w_i$) and
selects feasible items in that order. This heuristic is fast but, without
additional modifications, is **not guaranteed** to find the optimal 0–1
knapsack solution or achieve a universal 50% approximation bound.

```{r greedy}
greedy_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:800, ], W = 3500)
greedy_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:1200, ], W = 2000)
```

**Question 3: How much time does it take for $n=1,000,000$ objects?**

This benchmark may use substantial memory and time. Run it manually to obtain
a machine-specific measurement; it is disabled for routine vignette builds.

```{r greedy-time, eval=FALSE}
set.seed(42, kind = "Mersenne-Twister", normal.kind = "Inversion")
big <- data.frame(
  w = sample(1:4000, 1e6, replace = TRUE),
  v = runif(1e6, 0, 10000)
)
system.time(gk <- greedy_knapsack(x = big, W = 3500))
```

The runtime for one million objects should be inserted here after running the
code on the target machine. For a sorting-based implementation, expected
complexity is $O(n\log n)$.

package root:

```{r run-tests, eval=FALSE}
devtools::test()
```

# 5 Profiling and optimisation

**Question 4: What performance gain could be obtained by improving the code?**

Profiling identifies bottlenecks, whereas benchmarking measures the size of an
improvement. The following `profvis` calls can be run interactively in RStudio.
They are included for reproducibility but not evaluated during HTML vignette
creation.

```{r profiling, eval=FALSE}
library(profvis)

profvis({
  brute_force_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:20, ], W = 3500)
})

profvis({
  for (i in 1:50) {
    greedy_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:2000, ], W = 2000)
  }
})

profvis({
  knapsack_dynamic(x = knapsack_objects[1:1000, ], W = 1000)
})
```

We demonstrate the benchmark workflow for our dynamic-programming implementation. No separate optimized version is included in this package. The following optional benchmark is not run when building the vignette.

```{r benchmark-dynamic, eval=FALSE}
library(bench)
x_bench <- knapsack_objects[1:1200, ]
W_bench <- 2000

benchmark_results <- bench::mark(
  original = knapsack_dynamic(x = x_bench, W = W_bench),
  check = FALSE,
  iterations = 20
)
print(benchmark_results)
```

# 6 Optional: parallel brute-force search

**Question 5: What performance gain could be obtained by parallelising brute-force search?**

This comparison requires the `parallel` argument in
`brute_force_knapsack()`. Parallel startup and communication overhead can
outweigh the benefit for small problem sizes.

```{r benchmark-parallel, eval=TRUE}
library(microbenchmark)

# 1. Create the same test data for both methods
x_test <- knapsack_objects[1:18, ]
W_test <- 3500

# 2. Check whether both methods return the same result
serial_result <- brute_force_knapsack(x_test, W_test, parallel = FALSE)
parallel_result <- brute_force_knapsack(x_test, W_test, parallel = TRUE)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(serial_result$value, parallel_result$value)))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(serial_result$elements, parallel_result$elements)))

# 3. Compare execution time
bm <- microbenchmark(
  serial = brute_force_knapsack(x_test, W_test, parallel = FALSE),
  parallel = brute_force_knapsack(x_test, W_test, parallel = TRUE),
  times = 5L
)
print(bm)

# 4. Calculate the observed speedup
serial_ns <- median(bm$time[bm$expr == "serial"])
parallel_ns <- median(bm$time[bm$expr == "parallel"])
cat("Serial median (seconds):", round(serial_ns / 1e9, 3), "\n")
cat("Parallel median (seconds):", round(parallel_ns / 1e9, 3), "\n")
cat("Parallel speedup:", round(serial_ns / parallel_ns, 2), "x\n")
```


### Parallel Brute Force

The `brute_force_knapsack()` function was modified to support parallel computing using the `parallel` argument.

- `parallel = FALSE`: runs the serial version.
- `parallel = TRUE`: runs the parallel version using at most two workers.

Both versions use the same 18 items and knapsack capacity (W = 3500). They return the same optimal solution.

We used `microbenchmark()` to compare their execution times, running each version five times.


**Benchmark results:**

| Method | Median time |
|---|---|
| Serial | `r round(serial_ns / 1e9, 3)` seconds |
| Parallel | `r round(parallel_ns / 1e9, 3)` seconds |

The observed parallel speedup was approximately
`r round(serial_ns / parallel_ns, 2)`x.

`r if (serial_ns > parallel_ns) {
  "The parallel version was faster than the serial version."
} else if (serial_ns < parallel_ns) {
  "The serial version was faster than the parallel version."
} else {
  "Both versions had the same median execution time."
}`

The results may vary depending on the problem size,
CPU performance, and parallel overhead.


# 7 Conclusions

This lab demonstrates how algorithmic complexity determines tractable problem
sizes. Brute-force search is exact but exponential, dynamic programming is
exact and pseudo-polynomial in capacity, and ratio-based greedy search offers
faster approximate solutions. Profiling helps locate bottlenecks, while
carefully controlled benchmarks can measure the effect of parallel computing.
The parallel implementation is controlled through the `parallel` argument of
`brute_force_knapsack()`, with benchmark results reported above.



```{r benchmark_table, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
library(microbenchmark)
library(tibble)
library(knitr)
library(knapsack)

n_vec <- c(12, 16, 20)
W_vec <- c(50, 200)
res_table <- tibble()

set.seed(123)

for(n in n_vec){
  for(W in W_vec){
    items <- tibble(
      w = sample(1:W, size = n, replace = TRUE),
      v = sample(5:50, size = n, replace = TRUE)
    )
    
    if(n <= 20){
      t_brute <- median(microbenchmark(brute_force_knapsack(x = items, W = W), times = 5)$time)/1e6
    }else{
      t_brute <- NA
    }
    
    t_dp <- median(microbenchmark(knapsack_dynamic(x = items, W = W), times =5)$time)/1e6
    t_greedy <- median(microbenchmark(greedy_knapsack(x = items, W = W), times =5)$time)/1e6
    
    row <- tibble(
      n_items = n,
      capacity_W = W,
      Brute_force_ms = round(t_brute,2),
      DP_original_ms = round(t_dp,2),
      Greedy_ms = round(t_greedy,2)
    )
    res_table <- rbind(res_table, row)
  }
}

kable(res_table,
      caption = "Median runtime (milliseconds) for different problem sizes n and knapsack capacity W. Parallel and serial brute-force performance is compared separately above.",
      col.names = c("Number of items (n)","Capacity W","Brute‑force (ms)","Dynamic programming (ms)","Greedy (ms)"))
```

Table above illustrates runtime behaviour across three algorithms.
Brute‑force with exponential \(O(2^n)\) complexity quickly becomes intractable as n grows beyond 30.
Dynamic programming scales linearly with n but slows down for larger knapsack capacity W due to its \(O(nW)\) pseudo‑polynomial complexity.
The greedy implementation maintains very low runtime across all tested sizes, but it only produces an approximate solution and does not guarantee the optimal result.
